report.source_text: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was performed which revealed a 5.1 × 7.5 × 3.9 cm heterogeneous hypoattenuating lesion in the left hepatic lobe extending up to the lesser curvature of the stomach with and centered over gastro-hepatic recess. There was a rim of peripheral enhancement around the lesion. A hypodense ring paralleling the rim of enhancement was seen around the lesion in the liver often referred to as a double target sign, which is characteristically seen in hepatic abscess. A curvilinear dense foreign body was noted extending from the left hepatic lobe lesion into the gastro-hepatic recess (Figs. 1 and 2). Notably, there was no extraluminal air or significant intraperitoneal fluid that would suggest an active leak from the stomach.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 43-year-old male initially presented with fever and headache for 5 days, along with elevated WBC, AST, and ALT, and mild right hemidiaphragm elevation on chest X-ray. He was discharged home after vital sign normalization. Three days later, he was readmitted with right upper quadrant and epigastric tenderness, and further elevated WBC, AST, and ALT. A contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5.1 × 7.5 × 3.9 cm heterogeneous hypoattenuating lesion in the left hepatic lobe consistent with a hepatic abscess, and a curvilinear dense foreign body extending from the lesion into the gastro-hepatic recess. Postoperative culture of the abscess grew Streptococcus anginosus and Actinomyces odontolyticus, confirming the infectious nature of the abscess, which was managed surgically and presumed to be secondary to stomach perforation by the foreign body.
